title: A logo is not a brand system
metaTitle: A logo is not a brand identity system
excerpt: A logo has to work small, on a dark surface, and beside type. The system around it is what keeps the next page from inventing a new palette.
alt: Two white smartwatch mockups on a plain light background, one showing the face and one the back. A logo has to stay clear on a surface this small.
caption: The mark has to survive a small object. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Is a wordmark enough to count as a logo?
faqs.answer: A wordmark is a logo. It still has to work small, on a dark surface, and beside a headline. If the only version is a delicate drawing on a white slide, you have a sketch, and the decisions around it have not been written down yet.

faqs.question: How do we stop the next page from inventing colors?
faqs.answer: Publish the short list of color jobs, with hex values, in the same place as the logo files. When a new page needs a color that is not on the list, add it once and name the job. A one-off hex in a single file is how a second palette begins.

faqs.question: Do we need a full brand system before the first website?
faqs.answer: You need the small version: type, the color jobs, the logo treatments, and the sentence beside the mark. You do not need a long book before the first page. The website is where you learn whether that short list holds.

markdown:
A brand identity system is the set of decisions that keeps the next page from inventing a new palette. The logo is one of those decisions. It is the one people ask for first, because it is the piece you can hold up in a meeting and call finished.

A mark can be beautiful and still leave the team unprotected. The second landing page, the pitch deck, the invoice, and the empty state in the product will each need color, type, and spacing. If those choices live only in someone's memory, every new file becomes a fresh opinion. The system is the memory, written down, with files attached.

## The mark has to pass three tests

Hold the logo at the size of a favicon and at the size of a browser tab. If the letterforms weld together, or a detail you loved becomes a speck, the mark only works on a presentation slide. Draw a simpler version for small sizes. Use it on the real surfaces. A system that ships the delicate version everywhere will look soft in the corner of a phone.

Place it on a dark surface and on a light one. A wordmark drawn in a single mid-tone will vanish on half the photographs you later choose. Plan the light version and the dark version together. Reverse treatments are part of the logo, in the same way a second weight is part of a typeface.

Set it beside a headline, a sentence, and a button. The mark has to share a line with words without shouting over them or shrinking into a stamp that no one reads. Alignment, clear space, and the minimum size are the practical rules. They take a few lines to write. They save a few dozen arguments.

The [Web Content Accessibility Guidelines](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) describe web content, including text and images, through four principles: perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. A mark that depends on one fragile color, or that disappears into its background, fails the perceivable test in ordinary use. You do not need a certification pass to take the hint. Draw the versions people can actually see.

## What the logo cannot remember for you

The logo does not choose the text color of a paragraph. It does not choose the typeface of a form label. It does not decide how much space sits between a headline and the sentence under it. Those are the decisions that make a second page feel related to the first.

Write them as a short list with jobs, not as a mood:

- A background color and a text color that you have checked on a phone in daylight.
- One accent, used for the action, and a quiet support color for lines and secondary labels.
- A headline face and a text face, with the sizes you will actually use.
- The logo files: small, large, light ground, dark ground, and a single-color version.
- The sentence the company is willing to repeat beside the mark.

That list is the system in its smallest honest form. A later article goes further into how small it must stay if a team is going to use it. Here, the point is the boundary. If a new page needs a choice that is not on the list, the choice gets added once, named, and then reused. It does not get improvised in the file and forgotten.

## How the next page goes wrong

The failure is rarely dramatic. Someone needs a diagram. The accent feels too bright for a chart, so they pick a new blue. The diagram looks fine alone. Next to the homepage it looks like a guest. A month later the app, the site, and the sales deck are three cousins who claim a family resemblance no one can point to.

The same drift happens with type. A slide tool substitutes a default face. An engineer installs a close match because the license for the brand face was never shared. An illustrator draws letters by hand for a social image. Each substitution is reasonable in isolation. Together they dissolve the mark's surroundings, which is where people actually read.

Fix drift at the moment it appears. Ask which decision is missing, add it to the list, and replace the one-off. A system that grows by a line when reality demands it will stay true. A system that grows by a new PDF every quarter will be ignored.

## Files, names, and the surfaces that matter

Name files for the job. `logo-dark.svg` and `logo-light.svg` tell the truth. `final-FINAL-v7.png` does not. Export SVG for the interface and a plain PNG for places that still refuse vectors. Include the favicon sizes you will actually upload.

Record the hex values next to the use names. Record the font family, the weights, and the two or three sizes a page needs. Put the logo's clear space in a sentence: "Leave at least the height of the mark on every side," or whatever rule you mean. A picture of clear space helps. The sentence is what someone follows at midnight.

Apply the set to three surfaces before you call it done. A homepage. A single product screen or a one-page sales sheet. An email or a document header. If the mark, the type, and the colors survive all three without a new invention, you have a system. If they survive only the homepage, you have a poster.

Public work is a useful reminder of range. A calm brand site and a dense product interface can share a family if the type, the color jobs, and the sentence stay stable. They will look like two companies if each surface is allowed its own palette.

## What you can leave out of the first system

Leave out alternate logos for every season, a library of illustrations you have not commissioned, and a motion piece that exists to make the guidelines feel expensive. Those extras photograph well. They do not keep the next page honest.

Leave out rules you will not enforce. "Always use the accent at 12% opacity for backgrounds" is a rule that dies the first time someone is in a hurry, unless a component already encodes it. Prefer fewer rules that are visible in the files.

The mark still matters. It is the signature. It has to work small, on a dark surface, and next to type, or the signature fails in the places a company actually appears. The system around it is what stops page three from becoming a redesign.
